dek_candidates: Your application money sits in your own bank account, not the company's — here's how ASBA and UPI make that work.
The money you pay for an IPO isn't really paid until you get shares. Here's the system that holds it safely.
ASBA lets you apply for an IPO without handing over your money upfront. UPI makes it instant.
design_notes: The intro beat uses a concrete ₹15,000 example to ground the abstraction immediately.
The 'mandatory-asba' section is kept short; it sets context but does not repeat the intro.
The 'hidden-parties' section is separated from 'upi-mechanism' to avoid overloading the reader. Each has a clear teaching purpose.
The 'after-allotment' section deliberately avoids T+3 deadlines; per brief, those go in a separate listing-timeline article.
No source_id is needed for common-knowledge narrative beats like 'if you get shares, money is debited'.

beats.beat: If you get shares: the SCSB debits the blocked amount and the money moves to the issue account. You see the deduction in your statement.
If you don't get shares: the block is released automatically. The money stays in your account; it was never actually paid.
Ground with a brief mention that SEBI has set timelines for unblocking and compensation for delays, but do not detail the T+3 mechanics — those belong in a separate article.

after-allotment.heading: What Happens After Allotment
after-allotment.purpose: Explain the two outcomes: debit on allotment, release on non-allotment. Avoid detailed timelines.

beats.beat: Define SCSB (Self-Certified Syndicate Bank) — the bank where the investor's account is held. It blocks the amount and later debits it on allotment.
Define Sponsor Bank — a SEBI-registered banker to the issue, appointed by the issuer as a conduit between stock exchanges and NPCI. It pushes the mandate requests to UPI.
Define NPCI — the umbrella organization that runs UPI. It routes the mandate and settles payment instructions between sponsor bank and SCSB.
Summarize the flow: investor approves mandate → sponsor bank sends collect request via NPCI → SCSB blocks funds in investor's account.

hidden-parties.heading: Who Are the Invisible Parties?
hidden-parties.purpose: Explain roles of SCSB, sponsor bank, and NPCI in the UPI-ASBA flow.

beats.beat: Open with the concrete experience: you apply for ₹15,000 worth of shares. That amount is blocked in your bank account, not paid away. It stays yours until allotment is decided.
State the plain definition: ASBA = Application Supported by Blocked Amount. You authorize your bank to block the application money in your own account, not transfer it to the company.
Ground: quote the Master Circular definition verbatim from ICDR Reg 2(1)(d).

intro.purpose: Define ASBA in plain terms and set the core idea: money is blocked, not debited.

beats.beat: State that ASBA is mandatory for all categories of investors in both public and rights issues. Quote Master Circular 'All investors shall use ASBA facility'.
Briefly describe what the old system looked like: investors used to give cheques or transfer funds to the issue account, money was held by the registrar. ASBA eliminates that risk.

mandatory-asba.heading: ASBA Is Now Mandatory for Everyone
mandatory-asba.purpose: Explain that all investors—retail, HNI, institutional—must use ASBA. Contrast with old system where payment was upfront.

beats.beat: State the own-account rule: you must use only your own bank account and only your own linked UPI ID. Third-party accounts lead to rejection. Ground with Chapter 10 para 8.x.
Add the PAN requirement: SCSB must ensure PAN on the application matches PAN linked to the bank account. Mismatch makes the application invalid.
Give a concrete consequence: if you apply using your father's bank account or UPI ID, the application will be rejected, even if the PAN is correct.

own-account-pan.heading: Your Bank Account, Your PAN, Your UPI ID
own-account-pan.purpose: Explain the own-account rule and PAN matching requirement.

beats.beat: Explain that retail investors applying through an intermediary (syndicate member, stock broker, registrar, depository participant) can use UPI to block funds. Investor enters UPI ID and approves a mandate on phone.
Describe the mandate: a collect request is sent to the investor's UPI app; upon approval, the amount is blocked by the SCSB, not debited.
Ground: quote Master Circular Chapter 10 para 3.1 on UPI allowing facility to block funds at time of application.

upi-mechanism.heading: UPI: Blocking Funds With a Single Tap
upi-mechanism.purpose: Introduce UPI as a payment mechanism for retail investors, explain the mandate flow, and define sponsor bank role.
